title: Vasco da Gama's First Voyage to India
intro: King Manuel I of Portugal chose Vasco da Gama to lead an armada of three ships and a supply ship round the Cape of Good Hope to India, carrying out a plan begun under King John II. The Portuguese wanted spices, which were costly to bring overland.
ending: Only 55 of the 148 men of the armada survived the voyage, and the São Rafael was burnt. Da Gama reached Lisbon on 31 August 1499 and King Manuel I gave him the title of Don and great rewards.

stops.text: The expedition began on 8 July 1497, on the Lisbon shipping line towards Cabo Verde. The crews numbered up to 170 men, with one ship carrying supplies for three years.
stops.quote: Thus began the expedition on 8 July 1497. The Lisbon shipping line to Cabo Verde was the usual one

stops.text: Near the bay of St Helena the crews made contact with people who ate sea lions, whales, gazelle meat and herbal roots. They wore fur, carried wooden spears with animal horns, and played flutes in a coordinated manner.
stops.quote: Contact was made near the bay of St. Helena with tribes who ate sea lions, whales, gazelle meat and herbal roots;

stops.text: The ships crossed into Mozambique, where the crews saw palm trees yielding coconuts. According to Damião de Góis, the São Jorge padrão was set up here to affirm Portuguese sovereignty, so that later explorers could not take the land for themselves.
stops.quote: They crossed into Mozambique with palm trees yielding coconuts.

stops.text: From Malindi the Indian Ocean was crossed on a direct passage to Calicut. According to Damião de Góis, the Holy Spirit padrão was set up here, and it is the only one of the five to survive, as the Vasco da Gama Pillar.
stops.quote: The coastal route until Malindi and direct passage from this port to Calicut

stops.text: The fleet reached Kappakadavu, near Calicut in the present Indian state of Kerala. Scurvy had been felt acutely while crossing the Indian Ocean.
stops.quote: On 17 May 1498 the fleet reached Kappakadavu, near Calicut, in the current Indian state of Kerala

stops.text: Negotiations with the Zamorin were difficult: the gifts were too poor, and Arab merchants resisted competition. Da Gama won an ambiguous letter of trading rights, then left without warning when the Zamorin demanded collateral, leaving a few Portuguese to start a trading post.
stops.quote: Negotiations with the local governor, Samutiri Manavikraman Raja, Zamorin of Calicut, were difficult.

stops.text: Da Gama fell behind on Terceira Island, preferring to stay with his brother, who was seriously ill, while the caravel Berrio went on to Lisbon.
stops.quote: Vasco da Gama had fallen behind on Terceira Island, preferring to stay on with his brother who was seriously ill

stops.text: Nicolau Coelho brought the Berrio into the Tagus on 12 July 1499 with the news that the Portuguese had reached India by sea. Da Gama returned home on 31 August.
stops.quote: On 12 July 1499, after more than two years since the beginning of this expedition, the caravel Berrio entered into the river Tagus, commanded by Nicolau Coelho

notes: The article is short and mostly undated. Dates for St Helena Bay (1497) and for Mozambique, Malindi and Calicut (1498) are inferred from the voyage's span and the 17 May 1498 arrival; it gives none. Left out: Cabo Verde (only named as the usual route, nothing happened there; wp would be the country), the Bons Sinais river (a river), Ilhéus (padrão Santa Maria, place unclear). The article says they raided ships for pilots and used or traded the prisoners but names no place, so this is in notes only: 'To gather pace, they raided ships in search of pilots. With the prisoners, the Captain-General could trade, or put them to work.' Calicut stop 'by land' is the short move from Kappakadavu. Lisbon as the start is inferred from the Lisbon shipping line. Terceira stop date 1499 only.
